sources.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups (author-hosted draft, 338 pp.)
sources.reading_verification: Downloaded the complete author-hosted 338-page PDF (1,838,207 bytes) and extracted its full text with mutool; read Ch. 5 §§5.1–5.5 in full (printed pp. 209–242), Ch. 3 §3.4.3 Example 3.4.15 (printed p. 119) and Ch. 7 §§7.2–7.3 (printed pp. 287–289). Running heads give printed page numbers; the theorem, corollary, lemma, exercise and example numbers quoted above are the printed ones. The design locator 'Ch. 5 §§5.4–5.5, pp. 230–242' is contained in this range.

contents.name: §5.1 An example: the circle group (matrix coefficients of S^1 are the Fourier modes; Fourier series is Peter-Weyl for T)
contents.support: The circle model of the general theorem, matching the coefficient basis with the integer characters.

contents.name: §5.2 The Haar measure and the regular representation of a locally compact group
contents.support: The published regular-representation supplier used here; Haar existence and uniqueness are the published supplier page.

contents.name: §5.3 The analogue of the group algebra (the action of L^1 functions on a unitary representation; approximate identity)
contents.support: Definition and basic properties of the L^1 action used in the existence lemma and in Parseval.

contents.name: Theorem 5.4.1 (Peter-Weyl): L^2(G) is the Hilbert direct sum of the coefficient blocks of the finite-dimensional irreducibles
contents.support: The L^2 completeness statement; the decomposition form is consumed by the regular-representation item.

contents.name: Lemma 5.4.3 (a finite-dimensional subrepresentation of the regular representation consists of continuous functions)
contents.reason: Kowalski needs this lemma only for the alternative route that identifies coefficient spaces with isotypic components of the regular representation; this pair proves uniform density first and derives L^2 completeness from Parseval equivalences, so the lemma is not consumed and is retained as source history.

contents.name: Corollary 5.4.2 (irreducibles are finite dimensional; unitary representations are Hilbert direct sums of irreducibles)
Lemma 5.4.7 (every nonzero unitary representation contains a nonzero finite-dimensional subrepresentation)
Exercise 5.4.4 (groups with a faithful finite-dimensional representation) and Exercise 5.4.6 (separation by compact operators)
contents.support: Exercise 5.4.6(1) is the same separation statement, proved in its compact-operator form; this pair's proof isolates the spectral-piece argument.

contents.name: Corollary 5.4.8 (separating points and completeness criteria, including the Plancherel form)
Proposition 5.4.9 (Frobenius reciprocity for compact groups)
contents.reason: Induction, rho-functions and Frobenius reciprocity for compact subgroups are commissioned for the later induced-representations page (RG-23); this pair does not consume them.

contents.name: Lemma 5.5.2 (inner products of matrix coefficients: Schur orthogonality with the 1/dim constant)
contents.support: The published orthogonality theorem is the supplier of the normalization used for the coefficient basis.

contents.name: Theorem 5.5.1 (character theory: orthonormal class functions, isotypic projection formula, multiplicity formula)
contents.support: This pair consumes only the orthogonality and projection/Plancherel consequences; the class-function basis is not built here.

contents.name: Example 3.4.15 (the regular representation of R contains no irreducible subrepresentation)
§7.2 and §7.3 (global differences for noncompact groups; the regular representation as a direct integral (7.4))
contents.reason: General measurable Hilbert fields, direct-integral decomposition (7.4), uniqueness and type-I theory are later RG-26 material. The current counterexample preserves and now proves its special scalar R Fourier model locally from published Plancherel, translation and density; that explicit scalar model is included separately and does not assume the general theorem.

contents.name: §7.3 scalar Fourier model of the regular representation of R
contents.locator: printed pp.288–289; special scalar case verified locally from earlier Plancherel/translation interfaces
contents.support: Complete local proof identifies measurable square-integrable scalar sections with L2(dxi), uses exp(-2piitxi) fiber actions, and proves Fourier intertwining by density. Individual spatial characters have modulus1 and are not in L2; scalar Hilbert fibers remain C.

sources.title: David A. Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups (MIT lecture notes, 12 pp.)
sources.reading_verification: Downloaded the author-hosted PDF (148,075 bytes, 12 pages) and extracted its full text with mutool; read the notes completely, including the opening discussion of compact groups that are not Lie groups and all numbered results 2.3–2.17.

contents.name: Opening discussion (pp. 1–2): compact groups that are not Lie groups; profinite Galois groups, Z_p and GL(n,Z_p)
Definition 2.3 (operator-valued Fourier transform of a measure at an irreducible representation)
contents.reason: The operator-valued Fourier transform and the algebra of operator fields belong to the C*-algebraic unitary-dual development, not to this pair's Hilbert-space Peter-Weyl theorem.

contents.name: Theorem 2.6 (the Fourier transform is an algebra homomorphism on convolution of measures)
contents.reason: Convolution-algebra duality is commissioned for the C*-algebra page; the present pair uses the Hilbert-space form of Peter-Weyl.

contents.name: Proposition 2.8 (translation covariance of the operator-valued Fourier transform)
contents.reason: This is the operator-field form of translation covariance; the present pair proves only the convolution-operator commutation needed for the spectral argument.

contents.name: Definition 2.10 and Proposition 2.11 (inverse Fourier transform; its range is the span of the matrix coefficients)
contents.support: The characterization of coefficient spans is what the representative-function definition records.

contents.name: (2.12): the K-finite continuous functions form a subalgebra of C(K) closed under the left and right actions
contents.support: Same algebra-closure content, proved here from the tensor and translation identities.

contents.name: Theorem 2.13 (Fourier inversion isomorphism; composition is multiplication by Vol(K)/dim V)
contents.support: The L^2 form and inversion consequences are consumed; the regular-representation form is the companion theorem.

contents.name: Corollary 2.16 (the normalized character measure maps to the mu-isotypic projection)
contents.support: The published isotypic projection of the complete-reducibility pair is exactly this operator; its properties are published.

contents.name: Proposition 2.17 (transpose duality between the inverse Fourier transform and the operator-valued Fourier transform)
contents.reason: Dual-pairing duality of the Fourier transform is C*-algebraic unitary-dual material; no step of this pair uses it.

sources.title: Terence Tao, 254A Notes 3: Haar measure and the Peter-Weyl theorem (2011), author-hosted lecture notes
sources.locator: 254a Notes 3, §§1–2: Haar measure, convolution, compact operators and the spectral theorem, through Theorem 6 and Theorem 7 (baby Peter-Weyl) and Exercise 22
sources.reading_verification: Downloaded the full author-hosted HTML page and extracted its text (about 65,000 characters of body text); read the sections containing the compact-operator/spectral-theorem setup, Theorem 6 (spectral theorem), Theorem 7 (baby Peter-Weyl) with its proof, and Exercises 17–24. Mathematical displays on the page are typeset images whose surrounding text states the results verbatim.

contents.name: Theorem 6 (spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators) and its proof
contents.support: The published spectral theorem is exactly this supplier; the notes confirm the finite-eigenspace/orthogonal-decomposition form used here.

contents.name: Theorem 7 (baby Peter-Weyl: for g != e there is a finite-dimensional invariant subspace of L^2(G) on which g acts nontrivially) and the spectral argument preceding it
contents.support: The separation proof used in this pair follows this argument: compact self-adjoint convolution operators, eigenspaces invariant under right translation, and the characteristic-function contradiction.

contents.name: Exercise17: no small subgroups in compact Lie groups
contents.support: Applied to U(n) in the full local profinite-representation factorization proof. Published inverse-limit kernels supply the other actual prerequisite.

contents.name: Theorem8 and Exercise20: Gleason–Yamabe and inverse limits of compact linear groups
contents.reason: The current profinite examples use their explicit inverse limit of finite groups and published no-small-subgroups in U(n), which are included separately. General compact-group Lie approximation/Gleason–Yamabe and inverse limits of arbitrary compact linear groups are not required.

contents.name: Exercise 22 (Fourier analysis on compact abelian groups: characters separate points, uniform density, orthonormal basis)
contents.support: Step3.1 gives the full compact-abelian specialization: unitary Schur makes every irreducible one-dimensional, hence a character; finite complete reducibility identifies R(K) with character span. Existing compact point separation, uniform density and coefficient orthonormal completeness prove all three Exercise22clauses, for general compact Hausdorff abelian K under inherited AC. No general LCA duality prerequisite is imported.

contents.name: Exercise 24 (characters separate points of a locally compact abelian group)
contents.reason: General LCA character separation is explicitly commissioned as lem-continuous-characters-separate-points-of-an-lca-group in FR17, row4, from the biduality theorem and FR16inversion; FR15only supplies elementary dual topology. The present compact Peter-Weyl proofs use their local compact matrix-coefficient separation; their abelian specialization is included separately and does not assume general LCA separation.

sources.title: Constantin Teleman, Representation Theory (Berkeley lecture notes, 60 pp.)
sources.reading_verification: Downloaded the author-hosted 60-page PDF (508,871 bytes) and extracted its full text with mutool; read §19.4–19.7 (unitarizability, completeness, Peter-Weyl statement), §19.8–19.14 (the U(1) model and its complete list of irreducible characters) and §22.5–22.7 including Lemma 22.6 on irreducibles of a product of compact groups with both proofs.

contents.name: §19.4–19.6 (finite-dimensional compact-group representations are unitarisable and completely reducible; orthogonality and norm-one character criterion)
contents.support: The published complete-reducibility theorem is the supplier used throughout the A page.

contents.name: §19.7 (Peter-Weyl statement: L^2(G) is the Hilbert direct sum of the End(V) over the finite-dimensional irreducibles, with the explicit inversion and inner product)
contents.support: Independent statement of the regular-representation decomposition with the dim V normalization of the inner product.

contents.name: §19.13–19.14 (the characters z -> z^n form the complete list of irreducibles of U(1); Fourier modes)
contents.support: Identifies the circle's irreducible characters and hence its Peter-Weyl basis.

contents.name: Lemma 22.6 (for a product of compact groups the irreducibles are the tensor products of irreducibles of the factors), with the character-theoretic and complete-reducibility proofs
contents.support: The finite-product input for the finite-coordinate description of the infinite-product dual.
